h1:
Khao Chin Lae, Lopburi
Limestone Mountain & Winter Sunflower Fields
intro: Khao Chin Lae is an oddly shaped limestone mountain that rises out of the flat fields just outside Lopburi town. When winter rolls around, the land at its base turns into a sea of golden sunflowers stretching to the horizon, with the mountain standing behind it as a backdrop. This is a practical guide to visiting Khao Chin Lae — when the flowers bloom, the viewpoint, the best photo angles, the entry fee, and how to get there.

blocks.html: Khao Chin Lae is a lone limestone outcrop sitting outside Lopburi town toward Phatthana Nikhom district, roughly 10–20 km from the city. The mountain itself has steep rock faces that climbers from elsewhere know well, but what brings everyday visitors out here is the sunflowers that grow around its base in winter. It's a rare sight in central Thailand — a wide carpet of golden flowers with grey limestone cliffs rising right behind it.

The sunflower fields around Khao Chin Lae start blooming from late November and last through mid-January each year. The peak — when the flowers are at their fullest and the plants are tallest — is usually December. If you're coming specifically to see the fields in full yellow, December through early January is your safest bet.

blocks.title: Check before you head out
blocks.html: The fields don't all bloom at once — many farmers stagger their planting, so some plots flower earlier and some later. Before you go, search for the 'Khao Chin Lae sunflower fields' page on social media or a local farm's page for the latest photos, so you don't end up at a plot that's just been cut or hasn't bloomed yet.

blocks.text: What the fields are like and what you'll find

blocks.html: The sunflower fields around Khao Chin Lae cover several hundred rai in total, spread across many plots run by different owners. Some are set up as tourist farms with photo props; others are villagers' fields that simply open to visitors. The one thing every plot shares is the limestone mountain in the background, which gives the photos here more depth than sunflowers on flat, open ground.

items: Multiple sunflower plots — some farms set up photo corners with windmills, wooden arches, and swings; others are open village fields. You can wander through several styles in a single day.
Limestone backdrop — Khao Chin Lae and the hills beside it sit behind the fields, so almost any angle puts the mountain in the frame.
Roasted sunflower seeds — vendors sell roasted sunflower seeds and sunflower honey as cheap, easy souvenirs.
Parking and farm cafés — the bigger farms have parking, drink stands, snack stalls, and toilets.

blocks.html: Entry to most of the sunflower fields runs about 20 THB per person (some farms bundle parking into that). It's a small price for a whole field of flowers. Beyond just walking around and taking photos yourself, many farms offer a few extras.

items.name: Walk and shoot on your own
items.blurb: The best basic option. Follow the paths through the plot and take all the photos you want with the flowers and the mountain. Early morning gives soft light, and the flowers face the rising sun just right.

items.name: Tram ride around the field
items.blurb: A small tram loops around the plot so you can see the field from several angles without walking far. Good if you've brought older relatives or small kids.

items.name: ATV / farm tractor rental
items.blurb: Some farms rent ATVs and small farm tractors to ride around the fields — both for the photo angles and the fun. A good fit for groups of friends or younger visitors.

blocks.text: Wat Khao Chin Lae and the hilltop viewpoint

blocks.html: On the mountain side sits Wat Khao Chin Lae. What many people come for is the long staircase that climbs the mountain (over 400 steps), ending at a large pink-and-white Buddha image you can spot from far off. At the top you get an elevated view looking down over the sunflower fields, the surrounding limestone peaks, and the wide Lopburi plains. It's a viewpoint worth the effort — and if you come in winter, you'll see the yellow carpet of the fields from up high too.

blocks.title: Make the climb easier
blocks.html: The staircase is fairly steep with little shade along the way. Go in the early morning or late afternoon when the sun isn't harsh, bring water, wear comfortable shoes, and take it in stages — there's no rush.

Another side of Khao Chin Lae that casual visitors may not know about: the limestone cliffs are a rock-climbing spot known to both Thai and foreign climbers. There are several climbing zones — for example, an easy-to-reach shaded zone and a zone near the temple that takes a bit of a hike. Routes range from beginner to hard. If you're keen to climb, go with a group or a school that has the gear and an experienced lead — this isn't something to attempt on your own without experience.

blocks.text: Where to pair it with next

blocks.html: Khao Chin Lae is in the Phatthana Nikhom area, which has several other nature spots within an easy drive — plenty to string together into a single day trip.

items.name: Pa Sak Jolasid Dam
items.blurb: Thailand's largest earthen dam, with a viewpoint along the crest. Late in the year a train runs across the water over the reservoir — a great photo.

items.name: Phatthana Nikhom viewpoints
items.blurb: Same area as Khao Chin Lae, with other sunflower plots and mountain-view spots to stop and shoot along the way.

blocks.text: How to get to Khao Chin Lae

items: Drive yourself — the easiest way. About 20–30 min from Lopburi town. Just open your map and search 'Khao Chin Lae sunflower fields' or 'Wat Khao Chin Lae'; the farms have parking.
From Bangkok — about a 2.5-hour drive, doable as a day trip out and back. A good winter-weekend trip.
Private car / taxi — if you arrive in Lopburi by train or bus, you can hire a songthaew or taxi in town to take you to the fields and wait to bring you back.
Go in the morning — the sunflowers face the morning sun, the light is soft for photos, and it's not yet hot. Aim to reach the fields around 8–10 a.m.

faq.q: What month do the Khao Chin Lae sunflowers bloom?
faq.a: They bloom from late November through mid-January each year, with the fullest fields and tallest plants usually in December. Check recent photos from local pages before you go, since the plots are planted in stages and don't all bloom at the same time.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee for the Khao Chin Lae sunflower fields?
faq.a: Most charge about 20 THB per person, and some farms include parking. Extras are available too, such as a tram ride around the field for about 20 THB and ATV rental from around 200 THB if you want to roam the plots.

faq.q: Can you climb up the mountain for the view at Khao Chin Lae?
faq.a: Yes. On the Wat Khao Chin Lae side there's a staircase of over 400 steps up to a large Buddha image on the mountain. The top is a viewpoint looking down over the sunflower fields and the surrounding limestone peaks. The stairs are fairly steep, so go in the morning or late afternoon and bring water.

faq.q: Is Khao Chin Lae far from Bangkok?
faq.a: It's about a 2.5-hour drive from Bangkok and can be done as a day trip. From Lopburi town it's another 20–30 min. A good fit for a winter weekend trip.

faq.q: Where can you go next after Khao Chin Lae?
faq.a: It's in the Phatthana Nikhom area, which has Pa Sak Jolasid Dam, the Phatthana Nikhom viewpoints, and other sunflower plots all within an easy drive — easy to combine into a single day trip.
